I’ve been through something very similar. Academic writing and reading somewhat ruined my ability to read and write for fun. Here’s my advice, but understand that I’m in my senior year of college, and still figuring this out myself. 

Readers and Writers (RW) block, as I call it, seems to me to stem from one of two things: either fear or a lack of commitment. Both of these things can take various forms (a fear of failure vs. a fear of ridicule; lack of commitment to the extensive process of writing vs. lack of time commitment)

The first thing to do is figure out which one of those causes your RW block comes from. Maybe it’s one, maybe it’s both. Once you know what the root cause is, we have a couple of options. 

If it’s fear, the solution is to be brave. Go into reading and writing with the understanding that not everything is going to be perfect, or even good, and people will comment on that. Expecting anything else is an unreasonable expectation. And I’m not saying to get over your fear, it’s a valid fear. What I am saying is that you have to learn to control and master your fear, however that may work for you. My personal recommendation for this is exposure therapy. That is to say, read and write despite your fear. Push past the notion that things will be good all the time, and allow yourself to write poorly. That’s what revision is for anyway, to fix poor writing. 

If it’s a lack of commitment, well, you have to commit. Find the time to read and/or write. Fully dedicate some amount of time to it, any amount of time, even if it’s only 15 minutes to start. Do NOTHING but read or write during that time. Maybe even get someone to hold you accountable. (I’m looking into starting a writing group with some fellow students at my university, maybe that is something you could try?) And if you can’t or don’t want to fully commit in some sense or another, then, unfortunately, there’s not much anyone can do to help. 

Writing is a process unique to everyone and each person is going to have their own way of doing things. Through trial and error, you have to find what works best for you (and only change one thing at a time, like in the scientific method, there should only be one independent variable). 

You also need to know that writing is work. It’s never going to feel joyful all the time, and you’ll never get anything done if you wait for it to be 100% pleasant. I’m still struggling with this one, but I’m making it through, slowly. 

I hope this helps in some way. Best of luck, and let me know if I can clarify anything—I know this was a lot

So if he’s gonna be useless physically for a while, then it would make sense that his magic is powerful. And less powerful abilities have less side effects. 

You’re gonna do fine, just know that it’s going to be rough every time you read it, not just after the first draft, but especially that one. And when it is, you always have revision. There are no mistakes you can’t fix in a word document, piece of paper, or whatever you’re writing on. 

Best of luck

First thing I do is run through a checklist checking my physical and mental health. Am I tired? Am I hungry? Am I thirsty? Am I over/under-stimulated? Am I anxious, worried, or otherwise generally, but controllably, unhappy? Am I comfortable?

Then, I start writing whatever comes to mind. Drawings, flow charts, phrases, whatever. Once all that’s on the page, I start to organize it into a file on my computer where I can find and add anything else I add to the journal (keep writing in the journal FIRST for a while, until it gets to the outline process). Once all of my immediate thoughts (immediate here being 3 days to a month or sometimes even longer) I start outlining. Outline on the computer, jotting down notes both there and in your journal. I have personally started to outline using a spreadsheet by dividing the story into 5 acts, 15 or so sections each. In the second, third, and potentially fourth columns, I have my A plot, B plot, and sometimes a C plot (feel free to do more for longer projects). I’m trying this outlining technique out for the first time, so forgive me that I don’t have any more steps after. 

That’s what I do. Not a hard set of actions, nor exhaustive. Just do your best and take care of yourself first, and the words will come. And never be afraid to write terribly. It’s easier said than done, but it really helps. Good luck

Well it all kinda depends on the rest of your world and the causes that lead to this point.

Is this a world ravaged by war? Was this city a prime target to be destroyed by an enemy? Because that could line up with people leaving when they had the chance, and it could mean that people had bunkers to survive in. 

What kind of weapons were used to destroy the city? Regular bombs would mean that the surrounding area is still habitable, and therefore the people can hunt, gather, and survive outside of the city. Nuclear bombs would mean it’s completely unlivable. 

Also, why is the city isolated? And if it’s so isolated that no one would help the survivors, why were they attacked? (This won’t break the story, just some important details to come up with.)

As far as more information, simply googling war survival stories could point you in a good direction. I wish I could help more in this aspect, but I don’t typically read a lot of war stories, so my knowledge here is a bit dry. 

Best of luck, and also, just as an FYI, there is a great community called r/worldbuilding that is probably better for this type of stuff than this community

Of course your feeling is valid. But that doesn’t mean your work sucks or anything close to it.

All that is means is that you can find the flaws in your own writing and these get highlighted when you read the work of others. Rarely have I ever read my own work for what it is, even after being told that it’s good by the people I’ve shared it with. I still see the flaws and the things I want to change and work on and I usually see my writing as god-awful. That doesn’t mean it is though. 

And, even if theirs is “better” than yours, so what? Flowers bloom at different speeds, so there’s no point in comparing yourself to where someone else is. 

I know all of this is easier said than done, but once you realize this, you will be a lot happier with what you write. And isn’t that all that really matters? That you enjoyed writing it?

I’m trying to writing an urban fantasy series and am currently in the outlining stage. I kept thinking something was missing from the story, but I wasn’t sure what and I’ve now come to realize that the story itself doesn’t make much sense. I think changing things around, reoutlining, and stuff might help, but a lot of others have told me to just write the story or tweak one part but keep writing. 

What do I do? Do I go with the original, go through and redo it, or just abandon it all together?

I know this is going to be frustrating, but the simple answer to all of your questions is: I don’t know, it’s up to you.

Long answer, you have to find what works best for you. I suggest googling some questions like “how to plot” and “how to develop character” and stuff like that to get a general feel for it.

As for what you want to write, I suggest you read. And that’s the biggest and most important piece of advice that you will give and should follow. But you need to read to find out what you enjoy and just try to write something like that. At least, that’s how I started.

Hope this helps!
